title: Linking semivowel /w/ or /j/ between words
trigger: At a vowel-to-vowel boundary between two words in connected speech, insert /w/ if word one ends in a rounded/back vowel sound (u:, əʊ, aʊ) and /j/ if it ends in a front vowel/diphthong sound (i:, eɪ, aɪ) — judge by the final vowel SOUND of word one, not its spelling.

title: Short vs long vowel identification in a syllable
trigger: Isolate the target syllable's vowel sound and classify it against the short set (ɪ, e, æ, ʌ, ɒ, ʊ, ə) versus the long set (i:, ɜ:, ɑ:, ɔ:, u:) — decide by pronunciation/duration, ignoring how the letter is spelled.

title: Plural/-s ending allomorph: /s/, /z/, or /ɪz/
trigger: Check the final sound of the base word: voiceless consonant → -s pronounced /s/; voiced consonant or vowel → /z/; sibilant sound (s, z, sh, ch, j-sound) → an extra syllable /ɪz/.

title: Odd-sound-out: matching a target consonant phoneme
trigger: Say each option aloud and isolate the phoneme in question (e.g. /k/ or voiced-th /ð/ vs voiceless-th /θ/) — group words that share the identical sound and flag the one word whose spelling looks similar but whose actual sound differs.

title: Word-internal glide and consonant-cluster classification
trigger: Break the word into its phoneme sequence: spot a glide /j/ or /w/ appearing before a vowel to flag a semi-vowel, or count/identify the consonant sounds before the first vowel to classify the initial consonant cluster type.

title: Identify the noun(s) in a sentence
trigger: Scan each word and ask if it names a person, place, thing, or idea (including proper nouns); the noun is what the sentence is fundamentally 'about', not a describing or action word.

title: Classify a noun by its subtype (collective/concrete-abstract/countable-uncountable/number)
trigger: Test the noun against the specific rule asked: does it name a group (collective), can it be perceived by the senses (concrete) vs an idea (abstract), or can it be counted with numbers/'a' (countable) vs only measured (uncountable) — including nouns that look plural (ending in -s) but are actually singular or vice versa.

title: Determine a word's part of speech from its function in context
trigger: Ignore the word's usual dictionary category and ask what job it is doing in THIS sentence: naming something = noun, showing action/state = verb, describing a noun = adjective, describing a verb/adjective = adverb — the same word (e.g. 'decreases', 'even', 'yesterday', 'Dutch', 'err') can shift class depending on sentence role, and some words function as both noun and verb.

title: Spot the auxiliary (helping) verb in a sentence
trigger: Look for the verb that accompanies the main verb to build tense/aspect (is, has, will, does, etc.) rather than carrying the core meaning itself — it sits next to a main verb (often the -ing/-ed form) and signals tense/mood, not the action.

title: Identify which noun an adjective modifies
trigger: Find the adjective, then locate the noun it sits next to (or logically points at) in the sentence — an adjective must attach to a specific noun/pronoun, not float on its own.

title: Adjective degrees of comparison: positive/comparative/superlative
trigger: Identify which degree is being tested — positive is the base form, comparative ('-er'/'more') compares two, superlative ('-est'/'most') compares three or more — then convert between forms, watching for irregular patterns.

title: Choose the correct adjective vs adverb form for a blank
trigger: Check what the blank modifies — a noun needs an adjective, while a verb/adjective/another adverb needs an adverb (often adjective + '-ly') — then pick the form matching that target word, not just the word's meaning.

title: Identify adverbs and their subtype (manner/place/etc.)
trigger: Find the word modifying the verb and ask what question it answers — how (manner, often '-ly'), where (place), when (time) — to both spot the adverb and classify its type.

title: Identify the type of pronoun (interrogative, relative, etc.)
trigger: Check what role the pronoun plays in the sentence — interrogative pronouns (who/what/which/whose) introduce questions, relative pronouns introduce clauses, and so on — and match that function to its labeled type.

title: Identify the preposition in a sentence
trigger: Look for the word that links a noun/pronoun to the rest of the sentence, showing a relationship of place, direction, or time (in, into, on, at, by, etc.); it precedes a noun phrase to form a prepositional phrase.

title: Cloze passage: pick the word that fits the grammatical slot
trigger: Read the sentence around the blank and first identify what part of speech the slot needs (verb, noun, or adjective) from its position, then choose the option that matches both that grammatical role and the passage's meaning/tense.

title: Collocation matching: word + fixed partner
trigger: When asked to match a word to its collocating partner from an answer list, test each candidate pairing against the target word and pick the one that forms a naturally fixed English expression (e.g. 'sound advice', 'endless possibilities', 'moral support') rather than one that is merely semantically related.

title: Phrasal verb particle fill-in
trigger: When a blank needs only the missing particle/preposition to complete a phrasal verb, identify the base verb's intended sense from context (searching, colliding, weakening, rising, etc.) and choose the particle that idiomatically completes that exact verb+particle pairing, not just any grammatically plausible preposition.

title: Phrasal verb meaning identification
trigger: Given a definition or a context sentence, recall or infer the two-word phrasal verb whose figurative sense (not the literal sum of its parts) matches; for domain-specific sets like telephone talk (hold on, patch through, hang up) anchor to the situational script to pick the right verb.

title: Idiom direct meaning recall
trigger: Given a named idiom, recall its standard figurative meaning directly from memory rather than parsing it literally, and match it to the paraphrase option that captures that figurative sense.

title: Idiom lookup from a stated definition
trigger: Given a plain-English definition or paraphrase of a meaning, scan the option idioms and pick the one whose known figurative meaning matches the definition exactly -- treat this as a reverse lookup in your idiom-meaning bank.

title: Idiom cloze completion in a narrative sentence
trigger: Read the narrative/scenario sentence for its situational cue (mood, timing, effort, secrecy, wealth, success, etc.), then pick the idiom whose figurative meaning is the natural fit for that specific situation as a completion of the blank.

title: Idiom usage correctness judgment
trigger: Given a sentence that uses an idiom, first recall the idiom's true figurative meaning, then check whether the sentence's context actually matches that meaning -- mark it correct only if the situational sense aligns, not just because the idiom is grammatically well-formed.

title: Grammatical subject/object identification
trigger: Find the finite verb first, then apply the standard role test: the subject is what performs the action (active voice) or undergoes it (passive voice), and the object is what directly receives the action in active voice -- trace roles methodically from the verb rather than guessing from word order.

title: Mixed / one-off
trigger: For an isolated borrowed/Latin phrase meaning question, treat it as direct vocabulary recall of common Latin/foreign loanwords used in English (e.g. vice versa = 'the other way around').

title: Opening a phone call — greeting & asking for someone
trigger: When the blank opens the call, use a formal opening formula — receptionist offers help ('Good morning, how may I help you?') or caller states purpose politely ('Could I speak to X, please?' / 'May I ask who's calling?') — match register (formal for reception/business, casual for friends).

title: Naming call-quality problems — phrasal verbs & vocabulary
trigger: Recognize the phone-specific idioms for connection trouble: 'cut off' (disconnected), 'stay on the line' (wait, don't hang up), 'hang up' (end the call), 'rope in' (involve someone), 'breaking up'/'garbled' (unclear audio), 'could you repeat that?' (didn't catch it) — pick the phrasal verb or adjective that matches the described audio symptom, not a literal synonym.

title: Confirming you can hear / are still there
trigger: For 'Are you there?' / 'Can you hear me now?' type blanks, the correct reply directly confirms presence or improved audibility ('Yes, I can hear you now' / 'Yes, I'm still here') — reject options that ignore the audibility question or answer something unrelated.

title: Register-appropriate acknowledgement — apology, thanks, small talk
trigger: When the blank is a short reactive turn (accepting an apology, saying thanks, answering 'how are you', or generically continuing the exchange), pick the shortest, most natural formulaic reply used in real spoken English ('No problem at all', 'You're welcome', 'I'm fine, thanks') over a wordy or overly formal option.

title: Transferring the call / requesting to hold
trigger: When someone must be connected to another person or asked to wait, use transfer/hold formulas — 'Could you hold on, I'll put you through' / 'One moment please, I'll transfer your call' — match the speaker's role (receptionist transfers; caller requests).

title: Formal register for appointment/service bookings
trigger: In service-desk contexts (clinic, office), use fully formal phrasing without contractions or casual fillers — state or ask preferences politely ('I would prefer...', 'Could you tell me if you are a new or returning patient?') rather than a casual or blunt equivalent.

title: Making, accepting, and timing social plans
trigger: For invitations and plans, match the function of the blank: accepting = enthusiastic agreement ('I'd love to come'), asking timing = a direct question ('What time does it start?'), suggesting = a proposal phrase ('Why don't we...?') — pick the option matching that specific function.

title: Closing a phone call politely
trigger: The final blank in a phone dialogue is almost always a closing formula — thanks plus goodbye ('Thanks for calling, goodbye' / 'Take care, bye for now') — pick the option that both closes and stays polite, not a mid-conversation phrase.

title: Mixed / one-off
trigger: One-off items: distinguishing command vs. request register from wording alone, and the fixed phrase for informing a caller they've dialled a wrong number — treat each individually rather than as a repeating pattern.

title: Subject-verb agreement with regular subjects
trigger: Find the true subject of the sentence, check if it's singular or plural, and match the verb/auxiliary (is/are, was/were, has/have, do/does) accordingly, ignoring any words in between.

title: Correlative conjunction agreement: proximity rule
trigger: With neither/nor, either/or, or 'or' joining two subjects, the verb agrees with the subject nearer to it, not the first one.

title: Special-subject agreement: collective, uncountable, quantity, indefinite
trigger: Identify the subject TYPE first (collective noun/company name = singular verb; uncountable noun = singular; expressions of quantity/money/time as one unit = singular; 'together with'/'as well as' phrases don't change the subject's number; indefinite pronouns like none/all-of take the number of the noun that follows), then pick the matching verb.

title: Cloze passage: subject-verb agreement across blanks
trigger: For each blank in a multi-blank passage, locate that blank's own subject (including existential 'there' and passive constructions) and pick the auxiliary/verb form that agrees with it in number, independent of the other blanks.

title: Cloze passage: tense consistency from context clues
trigger: Read the whole passage for time-marker and sequence clues (already/by the time/reported speech backshift) and pick the tense for each blank that keeps it consistent with the surrounding narrative timeline.

title: Cloze passage: past-narrative verb forms
trigger: In a story told in simple past, conjugate each verb to its simple-past or past-participle-after-had form to match the narrative's established past timeline.

title: Participle/gerund as noun modifier
trigger: When a verb is describing (modifying) a noun rather than acting as the main tensed verb, use its -ing (present participle) or -ed/-en (past participle) form instead of a finite tense.

title: Identify the grammatical feature in a given sentence
trigger: Instead of filling a blank, inspect the given sentence's verb/subject and classify it (name the tense, decide active vs passive, or pick out the word that carries tense and agreement) by checking the auxiliary and verb form used.

title: Stative verbs never take continuous form
trigger: Verbs of state (seem, know, own, love, believe, etc.) describe a condition, not an ongoing action, so they cannot take an -ing/continuous form even where a dynamic verb could.

title: Perfect continuous tense: has/have/had been + V-ing
trigger: For an action continuing up to a reference point (now = present perfect continuous, a past moment = past perfect continuous, a future moment = future perfect continuous), build the verb as (will) have/has/had + been + V-ing.

title: Simple/perfect tense selection from time-marker cues
trigger: Scan the sentence for a time expression (a few days ago, since last Monday, every day, etc.) and let it dictate simple past, simple present, or present perfect.

title: Subjunctive mood: wish + were
trigger: After 'wish' (or 'if only') for an unreal/hypothetical present state, use 'were' for all subjects, not 'was', even with I/he/she/it.

title: Modal verb function matching
trigger: Name the exact function the sentence needs (permission, obligation, ability, possibility/speculation, advice, offer, warning, logical deduction) and map it to the modal that conventionally expresses that function (can/could, must/have to, may/might, should/ought to, shall, will).

title: Single-word meaning-in-context substitution
trigger: When asked for the meaning/substitute/closest-in-meaning word for a term as used in THIS passage, ignore the word's common dictionary sense and re-read only the sentence containing it (plus the clause before/after) to infer sense from local context, then match the option that keeps the sentence's meaning and tone unchanged.

title: Antonym of a word drawn from the passage
trigger: First fix the passage-context sense of the target word (not a random secondary dictionary sense), then pick the option that is the opposite of THAT sense — with 'from list B' style questions, verify the pairing is a true antonym and not a near-synonym distractor.

title: Direct word-to-synonym list matching
trigger: These are standalone vocabulary-matching items (no passage sentence to disambiguate) — recall the word's most common general-usage synonym rather than a contextual one, and eliminate options that are synonyms of a DIFFERENT sense of the word.

title: Collocation: word paired with its natural noun
trigger: Test each option by mentally inserting it after the given adjective and judging which noun it habitually pairs with in standard English usage (e.g. 'critical mass', 'financial burden') — this is about fixed word-partnership, not meaning similarity.

title: Idiom / phrasal verb meaning in passage
trigger: Treat the idiom or phrasal verb as one unit of meaning (never decode it word-by-word); recall its standard figurative meaning and confirm it fits the surrounding sentence's emotional/logical register.

title: Cloze: best-fit word for a passage blank
trigger: Read the full sentence (and often the sentence before/after) around the blank, identify the required part of speech and register from the sentence's grammar, then pick the option that both fits grammatically and preserves the passage's tone/logic — do not pick on word familiarity alone.

title: True/False verification of one stated claim
trigger: Locate the exact sentence in the passage that the claim paraphrases, then check word-for-word whether the passage actually asserts it, contradicts it, or is silent on it — 'not stated' and 'false' are both judged False, only an explicit match is True.

title: Spot the false / NOT-true statement among options
trigger: Check each option against the passage one at a time like a checklist; three or four will be directly verifiable as true, so the answer is the single option that either contradicts the text or adds a detail the passage never states.

title: Direct fact/detail scanning (who, what, when, where)
trigger: Identify the concrete noun/number/name the question asks for, scan the passage for that exact keyword or its synonym, and lift the answer straight from the surrounding text — no inference required, just accurate locating.

title: Attribute a quotation or claim to its speaker/source
trigger: Trace the quoted or reported statement backward to the nearest dialogue tag or named source ('X said', 'according to Y') in the passage — the answer is whoever the passage explicitly credits, not whoever seems most logical.

title: Infer a character's motive, cause, or unstated condition
trigger: The answer isn't stated in one sentence — combine two or more nearby details (actions, descriptions, consequences) the passage gives about the character/situation to deduce the underlying motive or cause the question is really asking about.

title: Infer the author's argument, implied view, or causal claim
trigger: Look past the literal sentence to what the author is arguing or implying — trace the passage's stated cause-effect chain, comparison, or analogy to its logical conclusion, since the correct option restates the author's underlying claim rather than a quoted detail.

title: Identify the article's purpose or rhetorical strategy
trigger: Ask 'why did the writer include this element (example, quotation, statistic, structure)?' — match it to a strategy type (evidence, contrast, appeal to authority, anecdote); for 'NOT/does not' variants, confirm each listed strategy is genuinely present before eliminating it, leaving the one absent strategy as the answer.

title: Judge the passage's tone, register, or intended audience
trigger: Scan the whole passage (not one sentence) for cumulative cues — word choice (technical vs everyday), sentence formality, and assumed background knowledge — to classify its tone/register or infer who it is written for/about.

title: Resolve what a reference word or hedging modal points to
trigger: For 'this thesis' / 'that claim' style references, find the specific noun phrase the pronoun/demonstrative replaces in the preceding sentence; for a modal like 'could', recognise it signals the author is hedging/expressing possibility rather than asserting fact, and pick the option describing that grammatical function.

title: Mixed / one-off
trigger: No shared reading-skill pattern with other items this week — apply the specific rule the question names (here, standard A-Z dictionary/alphabetical ordering letter by letter).

title: Vocabulary meaning/synonym from audio context
trigger: Question asks for a synonym or meaning of a specific word used in the audio/stem: pin down the sense the word carries in that context (not just its dictionary sense) and match or eliminate options against that contextual meaning, using elimination on odd-one-out variants.

title: Grammar correctness in a heard sentence (agreement/comparatives)
trigger: Question tests whether a sentence 'as heard' is grammatically well-formed: check subject-verb agreement (is/are) or comparative-adjective form against the noun it modifies, and pick the option that is grammatically consistent, not just the one that sounds closest to the audio.

title: Pause/phrasing pattern matching in spoken sentence
trigger: Question shows several pause-marked versions of a sentence: mentally read each option aloud with its pause breaks and pick the one where pauses fall at natural phrase/clause boundaries (not mid-phrase), matching how the sentence would actually be spoken.

title: True/false verdict on a single stated claim
trigger: Question gives one claim and asks true or false: locate the exact sentence in the passage that addresses this claim and check it word-for-word against the claim (watch for negation, absolute words like 'only'/'always', or partial matches) rather than judging by general impression.

title: Select all true statements from a passage (MSQ)
trigger: Question asks to select ALL statements that are true (multiple correct answers): evaluate each option independently against the passage as its own true/false check, since options are graded separately and partial credit rewards catching each correct one without over- or under-selecting.

title: Specific fact/detail recall (who/what/when/why/how)
trigger: Question asks for one specific fact, cause, or figure mentioned in the audio (a why/when/how/what question with a single answer): scan for the keyword from the question stem in the passage and lift the fact stated immediately around it, rather than reasoning or inferring beyond what was explicitly said.

title: Counting syllables in short common words
trigger: Say the word aloud and count distinct vowel SOUNDS (not vowel letters) - each vowel sound is one syllable; e.g. destiny = des-ti-ny = 3 vowel sounds = 3 syllables.

title: Counting syllables in medium multisyllabic words
trigger: Break the word into pronounced vowel-sound units, folding any silent 'e' or vowel digraph into the syllable it belongs to, then total the count; e.g. lo-co-mo-tive = 4 syllables (final 'e' is silent, not a separate syllable).

title: Counting syllables in long or complex words
trigger: For longer words, mark every vowel sound including reduced/schwa syllables, and treat any diphthong (like 'oi' in oily) as a single vowel sound, then count the units; e.g. en-vi-ron-ment = 4.

title: Classifying word length by syllable-count label
trigger: First count the vowel sounds using the standard counting technique, then map the number to the label: 1=monosyllabic, 2=disyllabic, 3=trisyllabic, 4+=polysyllabic; e.g. erode = e-rode = 2 sounds = disyllabic.

title: Spotting monosyllabic words despite complex spelling
trigger: Ignore the number of vowel letters and consonant clusters; count only vowel SOUNDS - a word with several vowel letters that form one diphthong/blend (straight = one vowel sound 'ay') is still monosyllabic.

title: Identifying primary stress by dictionary pronunciation
trigger: When the word carries no stress-shifting suffix, there is no shortcut rule - recall/apply the standard dictionary stress pattern (the syllable pronounced loudest and longest); e.g. af-FIL-i-ate is stressed on the second syllable.

title: Suffix rule for stress shift (-ic/-ion/-ity/-ian/-ical)
trigger: Certain endings pull primary stress onto the syllable immediately before them: -ic/-ical, -ion, -ity, -ian all place stress right before the suffix; e.g. po-li-TI-cian (stress before -cian), pop-u-LAR-i-ty (stress before -ity).

title: Stress placement in compound words and phrases
trigger: In compound nouns, stress usually falls on the FIRST element (FOOT-ball); in hyphenated compound adjectives made of two content words, stress typically falls on the SECOND element (ice-COLD) - identify the compound type first, then apply the rule.

title: Noun-verb stress shift in two-syllable words
trigger: For many two-syllable noun/verb pairs, stress falls on the FIRST syllable when the word functions as a noun and on the SECOND syllable when it functions as a verb - check the word's grammatical role in the sentence first, then place stress; e.g. REB-el (noun) vs re-BEL (verb).

title: Detecting aspiration of voiceless stops p/t/k
trigger: A voiceless stop (p, t, k) is aspirated (strong puff of air) only when it begins a STRESSED syllable at a word/syllable onset; the same sound is unaspirated when it follows 's' or sits in an unstressed syllable - check stress position and preceding sound, not just the letter.

title: Classifying consonant clusters by position and size
trigger: Identify where the cluster sits (word-initial/onset vs word-final/coda) and count the consonant sounds pronounced together with no vowel between them to classify the cluster's position and size; e.g. 'fl' in flip is a 2-consonant initial cluster.

title: GD evaluation criteria and terminology recall
trigger: Recognize these as direct recall questions on Group Discussion fundamentals (skills assessed, terms like value-fit); match the stem against the standard list of GD evaluation parameters rather than reasoning it out.

title: Choose a/an by spoken sound, not spelling
trigger: Say the next word aloud: use 'an' if it starts with a vowel SOUND (an hour, an MBA) and 'a' if it starts with a consonant SOUND (a European, a long time), ignoring the written first letter.

title: Definite 'the' for unique or already-specified nouns
trigger: Use 'the' when the noun is unique, superlative-marked, or already identified by context (the Bradman of India, the least expensive); use a/an only for a non-specific, first-mention singular countable noun.

title: Match article/verb to countable vs uncountable noun
trigger: First classify the noun as countable or uncountable: uncountable nouns never take a/an or a plural -s and pair with singular verbs, so fix the article or noun-ending to match that class.

title: Quantifiers keyed to noun countability and polarity
trigger: Pick the quantifier by noun class and tone: many/few for plural countables, much/little for uncountables, 'a few/a little' = some (positive) vs 'few/little' = hardly any (negative), each = one-by-one vs every = as a group.

title: Memorized verb/adjective + preposition pairs
trigger: These prepositions are fixed idiomatic pairings with a specific verb or adjective (jump over, talk about, upset about, allergic to, good at, reason for) — recall the memorized collocation rather than reasoning from meaning.

title: Prepositions of time: since/for/at/on/before
trigger: Identify what kind of time expression follows: 'since' + a starting point, 'for' + a duration, 'at' + clock time, 'on' + a date/day, 'before/by' + a deadline — the noun's time-type dictates the preposition.

title: Prepositions of place and direction by spatial geometry
trigger: Visualize the physical relationship first: 'at' = a point, 'on' = touching a surface, 'in' = inside an enclosed space or a city/country name, 'to' = destination of movement, 'through' = movement across/inside a space — match the preposition to that geometry.

title: Single-word usage errors: negation, comparison, pronoun case, adverb form
trigger: Isolate the one suspect word and test it against its rule: no double negatives (not...never), only one comparative marker (better, not more better), subject pronoun as subject (I, not myself), and -ly adverb after action verbs (behaves friendly is wrong) — fix only that word.

title: 'One of the' always takes a plural noun
trigger: In 'one of the (most) + noun', the noun after 'the' must be plural even though 'one' is singular (one of the most popular dishes) — check the noun's number, not the subject's.

title: Sentence-editing checklist: parallelism, possessives, hyphenation, ambiguity
trigger: For rewrite/proofreading options, test each candidate against a checklist — matching grammatical structure across a list (parallelism), correct possessive apostrophe placement, a hyphen joining a compound modifier before its noun, and unambiguous placement of the modified phrase — and reject any option that fails one item.

title: Correlative connective pairing (not only...but also)
trigger: Spot a correlative pair marker (not only...but also, either...or, neither...nor) and check that the element right after the first word matches the grammatical structure being emphasized in the second clause — the correct choice keeps both halves parallel and places 'not only' immediately before the emphasized item.

title: Cause/reason connective selection and function
trigger: Spot that one clause explains WHY the other happens, then pick or identify the connective (because, since, due to, as a result of) that names that causal link rather than a contrast or addition marker.

title: Contrast/concession connective selection and function
trigger: Spot two clauses whose ideas oppose or concede each other, then pick or identify the connective (although, whereas, despite, nevertheless, however) that signals that opposition, checking the comma placement each connective type requires.

title: Other connective and transitional-word recognition
trigger: Pin down the exact logical relation the blank needs (a range: from...to/between...and; a noun-clause link: whether/that; a generic transition), then test a transitional word by deleting it — if the sentence's logical relation collapses without it, it is load-bearing and the identified relation, not a synonym match, decides the answer.

title: Punctuating direct and nested quotations
trigger: Locate exactly where the quoted speech begins and ends relative to the reporting clause; close each quoted segment with the comma/period belonging inside the quotation marks, capitalize the first word of a new quoted sentence, and switch to single quotes for a quote nested inside another quote.

title: Sentence mechanics: comma, apostrophe, conjunction errors
trigger: Scan the sentence for one specific mechanical fault at a time — a missing or misplaced comma, a missing apostrophe in a contraction, or two independent clauses joined without a coordinating conjunction (comma splice) — and apply the single fix that repairs just that fault.

title: Identifying and evaluating the topic sentence
trigger: Find the sentence stating the paragraph's main claim (usually the opening sentence), then judge its grammatical form (statement vs. question) and whether it genuinely previews everything the paragraph goes on to say — that single check settles form-identification and true/false questions alike.

title: Paragraph coherence: ordering, repetition, and conclusions
trigger: Trace the logical or chronological thread linking sentences (pronoun references, repeated key terms, cause-then-effect order) to fix the correct sequence, judge whether repetition unifies the paragraph, or check whether the final sentence effectively closes the argument it built.

title: Classify formal vs informal register
trigger: Check for salutation/closing formulas and structural conventions (e.g. 'Dear Sir/Madam', 'Yours faithfully', addressed to an authority) versus casual greetings and structure to classify the piece as formal or informal.

title: First-person 'I' and its effect on tone/objectivity
trigger: Judge first-person pronoun use by genre: in an objective article/report 'I' undermines impartial tone, but in an official letter 'I' is appropriate because the writer is a stated, accountable party requesting/reporting something.

title: Extract the functional purpose of specific content
trigger: Scan for direct action verbs, request statements, and lists of specifics to determine what the writer explicitly wants the reader to do or why that content is included (e.g. listing amenities to substantiate a complaint, listing details a brochure needs to fulfil its promotional purpose).

title: Identify urgency-conveying language
trigger: Look for time-bound phrases, intensifiers, and consequence statements (deadlines, 'immediately', 'urgent', negative outcomes if unaddressed) that signal the writer is conveying urgency.

title: Recognize argumentative strategy used or absent
trigger: Classify the rhetorical/argumentative strategy by checking what kind of support the writer leans on (cause-effect, comparison, definition, evidence/example) and whether a specific strategy (e.g. definition-based argument) is present or notably absent.
